strengths: DRE-BO-SSL provides a practically motivated combination of classifier-based Bayesian optimization and graph-based semi-supervised learning. Exploiting candidate geometry is particularly appealing when a fixed pool of unevaluated configurations is available.

The experiments cover continuous synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-embedding search task. Comparisons include GP-EI/UCB and several BORE/LFBO classifiers, with promising improvements, especially on NATS-Bench.

Twenty repetitions with reported means and standard errors provide useful evidence beyond individual successful runs. The appendices investigate bandwidth, threshold ratio, sampling distributions, unlabeled-set size, and computational effects of pool subsampling.

The acquisition-landscape visualizations communicate the intended failure mode clearly. The paper explains its relationship to BORE, LFBO, and established label propagation/spreading methods, and provides pseudocode and detailed benchmark constructions.
weaknesses: The central attribution of improvements to unlabeled data remains insufficiently established. Figure 12 shows that removing unlabeled points can improve performance substantially, including on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. Moreover, this ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main results learn beta and Figure 4 shows much larger values. A comparison against a tuned supervised kernel classifier with matched acquisition search and tie-breaking is needed to distinguish the benefit of transduction from the kernel model and bandwidth selection.

The cluster-based justification does not follow from the sampling procedure. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated locations does not ensure that regions of high sampling density have consistent objective-threshold labels, especially as the threshold changes during optimization. Appendix C acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. learning results do not apply to this sequential setting. Its discussion therefore provides intuition, but does not establish the claimed improvement in exploration or optimization performance.

Acquisition optimization is insufficiently specified to assess comparison fairness. Section 5 reports L-BFGS-B with 1,000 initializations, but does not clearly explain optimization over finite categorical pools or the corresponding procedure for tree-based baselines with piecewise-constant scores. These choices can materially affect the reported rankings. A random-search baseline and explicit controls for the random tie-breaking heuristic would also help establish the source of the gains.

Evidence for general high-dimensional optimization is limited. The continuous benchmarks are all two-dimensional, while the 64-dimensional MNIST features come from a network trained on 440,000 examples to predict the same digit identity that defines the objective. Although the optimization pool uses separate test images, this supplies unusually strong task-specific information and limits the experiment's generality.

Important reproduction details remain missing, including feature scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, bandwidth-optimization bounds and initialization, and MLP baseline training settings. These omissions matter because the method depends strongly on distances and bandwidth, and the experiments provide most of the support for the contribution.

A smaller mathematical presentation issue should be corrected: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1}W. This makes the intended propagation update in Equation (11) ambiguous.
